notes.meaning: Paul left the philosophers in Athens and walked about fifty miles west to Corinth. Corinth was a rich, bustling port city famous across the ancient world for trade, luxury, and wicked living. Paul chose this busy center because a strong church planted there could reach travelers heading across the whole empire.

In Corinth, Paul met a Jewish believer named Aquila and his wife Priscilla. They had recently been forced out of Rome because Emperor Claudius ordered all Jews to leave the city. Paul went to visit them and quickly formed a close partnership with them in ministry.

Paul lived and worked alongside Aquila and Priscilla because they shared the same craft of making tents out of leather or woven cloth. Jewish teachers were taught to learn an honest trade so they could support themselves. Paul worked with his hands so that no one could say he preached only to get rich.

On every Sabbath, the Jewish day of rest, Paul went to the local synagogue to discuss the Scriptures. He tried to persuade both Jewish listeners and Greek worshippers that the prophets pointed to Jesus. During the work week he earned his living, and on the Sabbath he focused on sharing the truth.

Silas and Timothy arrived from northern Greece, bringing encouraging reports about the believers there and financial help from other churches. Free from the constant need to make tents, Paul poured all his energy into preaching. He declared boldly to his Jewish hearers that Jesus is truly the Christ, God's promised King.

When many in the synagogue fought against his message and spoke insults against Christ, Paul shook out the dust from his robe as a warning. He told them they were responsible for their own ruin and that he had done his duty faithfully. From that day on, he focused his preaching on the non-Jewish people, called Gentiles.

Paul moved his teaching out of the synagogue and set up his work right next door in the home of Titus Justus. Titus Justus was a Gentile who already loved and worshipped the God of Israel. This nearby house made it very easy for open-minded synagogue visitors to come hear Paul.

Crispus, the chief ruler of the Corinthian synagogue, believed in the Lord Jesus along with his entire family. His decision was a major event in the city and moved many other Corinthians to listen. When they heard the good news, they also believed and were baptized.

The Lord Jesus appeared to Paul during the night in a vision to lift his spirits against rising danger. Christ told him to stop being afraid and to keep on preaching boldly without going silent. Even experienced leaders need God's comforting words when threats grow around them.

The Lord promised Paul that He would stay right beside him and keep any enemy from harming him. Jesus also explained that He already had many people in this corrupt city waiting to hear the message and be saved. That assurance gave Paul courage to face intense opposition with peaceful confidence.

differ.view: Christ's words describe God's elect, the people chosen for salvation before time began who were sure to be called to faith through Paul's preaching.
The Lord spoke prophetically about people in the city whom He foreknew would freely hear and accept the message.

notes.meaning: Paul stayed in Corinth for a year and a half, faithfully teaching God's word among the people. This was his longest time in any city up to this point in his travels. Because he stayed so long, he was able to establish a strong, lasting church in the middle of a pagan city.

When Gallio became the Roman governor of the region, hostile Jewish opponents joined forces to drag Paul to the public court platform. Gallio was a cultured man and the brother of the famous Roman writer Seneca. The accusers hoped this new ruler would shut down Paul's preaching for good.

The crowd accused Paul of persuading people to worship God in ways that broke the law. They worded their claim carefully so the Roman ruler might think Paul was starting an illegal religion against the empire. In reality, Paul was only preaching what God had promised in the Jewish Scriptures.

Just as Paul got ready to defend himself, Gallio stepped in and answered the accusers directly. The governor said that if Paul had committed a real crime, a fraud, or violence, it would be his job to listen to them. Since no civil law was broken, he saw no reason to hold a trial.

Gallio pointed out that their complaint was only about religious teachings, names, and their own Jewish laws. He told them to settle the quarrel among themselves because he had no interest in judging religious matters. He viewed their debate as unimportant hair-splitting.

Gallio dismissed the case and ordered the crowd to be cleared away from the judgment seat. His refusal to outlaw Paul's teaching gave the young church official protection under Roman rule as a lawful faith. God used a pagan ruler to keep His promise that Paul would not be harmed.

Angry at how things turned out, the crowd seized Sosthenes, the new synagogue leader, and beat him right in front of the court. Gallio turned a blind eye to the fight and did nothing to stop it. Sosthenes may have later turned to faith in Christ, since Paul later mentions a brother named Sosthenes in his letters.

Paul stayed in Corinth for many more days in peace before saying goodbye to the church family. He sailed for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila, stopping first at the harbor town of Cenchrea. There Paul had his hair cut short to finish a temporary religious vow of special devotion to God.

When the ship docked at the great port city of Ephesus, Paul left Priscilla and Aquila there to begin living and working. Paul went straight into the local synagogue during his brief stop to reason with the Jews about Jesus. Even when traveling, he used every spare moment to share the gospel.

The people in Ephesus were impressed by what Paul said and asked him to stay with them longer. Even though their invitation was friendly, Paul chose not to stay at that time. He was eager to reach Jerusalem to present his vow and celebrate the coming feast.

As Paul said goodbye, he promised that he would return to Ephesus if God willed it. Then he boarded the ship and sailed away. He knew that all human plans must submit to God's wise direction and timing.

Paul landed at the harbor of Caesarea and traveled up to Jerusalem to greet the church leaders there. After his brief visit, he headed north down to Antioch in Syria, where his sending church was located. This arrival brought his second long missionary journey to a safe close.

After spending some time resting and giving reports in Antioch, Paul set out on his third missionary journey. He walked across the regions of Galatia and Phrygia, visiting each town in order. His main goal on this trip was to build up and encourage the young believers he had led to Christ years earlier.

While Paul was traveling inland, a Jewish man named Apollos arrived in Ephesus. He was from Alexandria in Egypt, a famous world center of education and deep thinking. Apollos was a gifted public speaker who had a masterful understanding of the Old Testament Scriptures.

Apollos had learned the basic truth about the Lord and spoke with deep, burning enthusiasm. He taught what he knew about Jesus accurately, but his knowledge stopped at the baptism of John the Baptist. He knew that the Messiah had come to call people to repentance, but he did not yet know the whole story of Jesus' death, resurrection, and the Holy Spirit.

differ.view: Apollos had true faith and zeal but lacked the baptism in the Holy Spirit that empowered believers after Pentecost.
Apollos was a genuine believer who understood the call to repentance, but simply needed fuller teaching about Christ's saving work and resurrection.

notes.meaning: Apollos began preaching boldly in the Ephesian synagogue, where Priscilla and Aquila heard him. Seeing his great gifts and his lack of complete facts, the couple quietly invited him to their home and explained the full truth of God to him more accurately. This humble scholar was glad to learn from ordinary tentmakers.

When Apollos decided to cross over to Greece to minister in Corinth, the Ephesian believers encouraged him and wrote a letter asking the church to welcome him warmly. When he arrived, he was a tremendous help to the believers who had come to faith by God's undeserved kindness. He watered the seeds of faith that Paul had planted earlier.

Apollos debated the Jewish opponents in public meetings with great power and answered every objection they raised. Using the Old Testament Scriptures, he proved beyond doubt that Jesus is the promised Christ. His clear arguments gave great courage to the young Christian community.
